summary: Russia hits Kyiv's bridges in revenge for Kerch, Anthropic's shares jump then fade on day one, COP31's draft drops fossil fuels, and warnings grow on Gaza, Ethiopia and Ebola.

question.text: Today, death tolls in Ukraine changed through the day, and Reuters could not confirm the border clashes that monitors reported between Ethiopia and Eritrea. When early reports from a crisis disagree, what would make you trust one account more than another?

read.title: Analysis: Why Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge is such a big deal
read.summary: Explains why one bridge matters so much: a symbol of Russia's 2014 annexation, a supply line for its army in the south, and the background to today's Russian strikes on Kyiv's bridges.

topics.heading: Russia strikes three Kyiv bridges and cities across Ukraine after vowing revenge for Kerch
topics.summary: Overnight, Russian missiles and drones damaged three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv and hit Lviv, Kharkiv and other cities; Ukraine's prime minister says at least 8 people were killed nationwide.[^1][^3] Poland is checking whether something crossed into its airspace.[^2]

lead.title: 3 Kyiv bridges struck in massive Russian aerial assault on Ukraine

alsoReported.title: Explosion in Poland Sparks Airspace Breach Probe as Russian Attacks Kill Civilians in Ukraine
Russian attack kills six in Kyiv, three reportedly water utility workers, as ballistic strikes hit three Dnipro bridges

article: Overnight into Friday, Russia launched ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at Ukraine. In Kyiv, three bridges over the Dnipro River were damaged, and Mayor Vitali Klitschko told residents not to drive.[^1] Power, heating and water went out in parts of the city, and Ukraine says nine regions were hit.[^1][^2]

Casualty counts were still changing. Klitschko first said at least 3 people were killed in Kyiv, likely workers at the city water utility.[^17] Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi later said 6 were killed in Kyiv and 8 across Ukraine, with dozens hurt.[^3] Two people were killed at a railway station in Lviv, and a drone struck a hospital in Kharkiv, injuring four, local officials say.[^3]

The attack came a day after Vladimir Putin promised "retaliation" for Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge, the only road and rail link between Russia and occupied Crimea, and said he would not negotiate truces on energy or at sea.[^1] Ukraine hit that bridge three times between Nov 16 and 19.[^4] One expert quoted by the Kyiv Independent thinks repairs could take a year or more.[^5]

In Poland, officials are investigating whether unidentified objects entered its airspace early Friday after people near the village of Chmielek reported a loud explosion. Poland has not named a cause, but it raised air-defence readiness and briefly halted flights at Rzeszów airport.[^2]

Why it matters: bridges, power and water are what keep a city running in winter, and both sides are now targeting the other's transport links. My read: this round of strikes makes the energy and sea truces discussed in recent talks less likely soon. Watch Poland's findings, because any confirmed incursion into a NATO country raises the stakes.[^2][^4]
topics.differences: Death and injury counts differ between Kyiv's mayor, the city administration and the prime minister, and were still rising.[^3][^17] Putin calls the Kerch Bridge a purely civilian site; the US-based Institute for the Study of War disputes that, pointing to its military use.[^4] No Russian statement on the overnight attack had been found at the time of writing.

topics.heading: Anthropic shares open 34% above IPO price, then close up 17% on first day
topics.summary: Anthropic's shares first traded at $111.50 on Nasdaq, well above the $83 IPO price, then slid to close at $97.17.[^6] The company raised about $81 billion, the largest IPO ever, on a day when the wider market fell.[^7][^8]

lead.title: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock closes up 17% from initial price for $1.27T valuation in first day of trading

alsoReported.title: Anthropic stock soars over 20% in Nasdaq debut
Anthropic set to start trading after completing largest-ever IPO

article: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude models, began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. It sold 980 million shares at $83 each, above its earlier target range, raising about $81 billion, more than SpaceX's roughly $75 billion listing in June.[^8] (Note: Claude, which writes this brief, is made by Anthropic, so read this item with that in mind.)

The first trade, just before noon in New York, was $111.50, about 34% above the IPO price. Shares touched $115.10, then fell below $100 within about 20 minutes. They closed at $97.17, up 17%.[^6][^7] Valuations depend on how shares are counted, but all estimates put the company well over $1 trillion.[^6]

The wider market fell that day: the Dow was down about 1.7% and the Nasdaq about 1% during trading, and other AI stocks such as Nvidia slipped.[^6][^7] CEO Dario Amodei called machine intelligence "one of the seminal moments in human history" and said the company has been honest that the technology has real risks.[^8]

Why it matters: this is the first large AI lab owned partly by ordinary investors, so its share price will now act as a daily public vote on the AI boom. Analysts urge caution: a Truist study found more than half of 32 mega-IPOs fell at least 50% at some point in their first year, and one Truist strategist said the listing should not be seen as a verdict on AI.[^8] My read: one day of trading says little; the next few earnings reports will say more.

topics.heading: COP31's revised draft deal drops all mention of fossil fuels as talks near deadline
topics.summary: A new draft at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, removed every reference to moving away from fossil fuels and accepts warming may pass 1.5°C.[^9] Talks were due to end Friday, with climate finance still the main sticking point.[^10]

lead.title: COP31 negotiators publish revised deal text with no mention of fossil fuels

alsoReported.title: What's left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
COP31 delivers deals for host Turkey as climate diplomacy stalls

article: Nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the yearly UN climate summit. On Thursday, negotiators published a revised draft deal that removed both references to moving away from fossil fuels that were in Monday's first draft.[^9] Australia, which runs the negotiations in a shared arrangement with host Turkey, said the first draft was always meant to start broad and then narrow.[^9]

The new text accepts that warming could pass 1.5°C, the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, and calls for "deep, rapid and sustained" emission cuts. It also encourages more technology to remove carbon dioxide from the air.[^9] Separately, many countries back a pledge to get 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, though most have not formally signed it.[^11]

Leaders of vulnerable countries pushed back. Panama's environment minister said the world is "held hostage by the petroleum mafia", and Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley called overshooting 1.5°C a "debt of heat".[^11] Money for the poorest countries is the main dispute, and Reuters reported on Friday that an ambitious outcome looked unlikely. Turkey says it secured over $26 billion in deals while hosting.[^10]

Why it matters: every country must agree by consensus, so the final text shows what the world can agree on, not what scientists recommend. The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared in a COP outcome only in 2021.[^11] What's next: talks often run more than a day late, so watch whether fossil-fuel wording returns in the final deal.[^9]
topics.differences: Vulnerable states such as Panama, Barbados and the Marshall Islands want stronger action and more money.[^11] The presidency says narrowing the draft is normal.[^9] The articles read do not name which governments pushed to remove the fossil-fuel wording.

topics.heading: Trump's Board of Peace tells the UN that both Israel and Hamas are falling short in Gaza
topics.summary: The US-backed body overseeing Gaza's ceasefire says both sides have "fallen far short" of their commitments, and warns that a truce that delivers nothing visible cannot last.[^12][^13]

lead.title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel and Hamas for failure to end Gaza war

alsoReported.title: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action

article: The Board of Peace, set up under Donald Trump's plan to oversee the Gaza ceasefire that began on Oct 10, 2025, sent its second report to the UN Security Council this week. In 12 pages, it says both Israel and Hamas have "fallen far short", and that the gap between the deal and reality is the biggest risk to the process.[^12][^13]

The report faults Israel for blocking a planned interim administration of Palestinian experts and for not deciding on training and deploying Palestinian police. It says Israeli limits on supplies, together with funding gaps, have hurt preparations for winter floods.[^12][^13] It faults Hamas for taxing goods that enter Gaza. Hamas agreed in July to a plan for giving up its weapons, which Israel rejected.[^12]

More than 2 million people in Gaza live on about a third of the territory, mostly in tents, while Israel controls the rest.[^12] Reuters reports that more than 1,600 Palestinians and 5 Israeli soldiers have been killed since the truce began.[^12] Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled and Gaza is demilitarised.[^12]

Why it matters: the report puts on record that the ceasefire's next phase, rebuilding and new governance, has barely started. "A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely," it says.[^12] Israel is also between governments after last month's election.[^12] What's next: the report is due to be presented to the Security Council at the end of November.[^12]
topics.differences: Reuters gives weight to Hamas's taxes and the rejected disarmament plan, while Al Jazeera's report stresses Israeli aid limits and calls the war genocidal, a term Israel rejects.[^12][^13] Israel's government and Hamas did not immediately comment.[^12]

topics.heading: Ethiopia and Eritrea mass troops along their border, conflict monitors say
topics.summary: Conflict monitors report both armies gathering near the border and possible clashes near Badme; Reuters could not confirm the clashes, and Eritrea calls the reports propaganda.[^14]

lead.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea amass forces along border, heightening war fears, sources say

article: Ethiopia and Eritrea have moved large numbers of troops to their shared border, according to the conflict monitors ACLED and International Crisis Group and two people linked to militias in Ethiopia's Tigray region, Reuters reports.[^14] ACLED reported shelling and clashes near the town of Badme, and drone strikes on Nov 12 on what were likely Eritrean positions.[^14]

Reuters could not independently confirm the clashes, and a pro-government militia source in Tigray said there had been none.[^14] Eritrea's information minister called the reports "propaganda", denied sending troops into Ethiopia and accused Ethiopia of looking for an excuse to invade. Ethiopia did not comment.[^14]

Background: Eritrea split from Ethiopia in 1993, and the two fought a border war over Badme in 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands. They made peace in 2018. Relations soured as Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called for access to the sea for his landlocked country, which he says he wants by peaceful means. Since September, Ethiopia's army has been fighting Tigrayan rebels, and Ethiopia says Eritrean troops crossed in to help them.[^14]

Why it matters: a war between these two countries would draw in a region already strained by Sudan's war, near the Red Sea shipping lanes. A Crisis Group analyst called it "a dangerous scenario that could trigger a direct conflict".[^14] My read: this is a warning sign, not yet a confirmed war; the key test is whether independent reporters can confirm fighting.
topics.differences: Monitors ACLED and Crisis Group report a troop build-up and clashes; Eritrea calls this propaganda and denies its troops are in Ethiopia; Ethiopia has not commented.[^14] Ethiopia accuses Sudan and Egypt of backing the rebels, which both deny.[^14]

topics.heading: WHO says Congo's Ebola cases have doubled in three months to more than 11,000
topics.summary: WHO chief Tedros says the outbreak has passed 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths in eight provinces, with 400 to 500 new cases a week.[^15] Africa CDC says it is "still not under control".[^16]

lead.title: World News in Brief: Ebola cases double in DR Congo, chemical exposure starts before birth

alsoReported.title: Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo 'still not under control'

article: At a meeting of the World Health Organization's emergency committee on Nov 17, Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo now counts more than 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths in 67 health zones across eight provinces. Cases have more than doubled in three months, with 400 to 500 new ones each week.[^15]

Children make up more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths. Two-thirds of confirmed deaths happen outside treatment centres, a sign that many infections are found late.[^15] Kenya has 9 linked cases and 2 deaths, and Nigeria has one imported case.[^15]

This is the Bundibugyo type of Ebola, which kills about half of those infected and has no approved vaccine or treatment. It is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, after West Africa in 2014 to 2016.[^16] Two candidate vaccines are due to join a trial in the coming weeks, and the number of labs able to test has grown from 2 to more than two dozen.[^15]

Why it matters: Ebola spreads through close contact, so finding cases early is what stops it. Africa CDC's chief says more than 80% of new cases are outside known contact lists, and called donor coordination "a collective failure".[^16] Tedros criticised blanket travel bans, saying they hamper the response.[^15] My read: some early hotspots have slowed, but the overall trend is still up.
topics.differences: Africa CDC stresses that the outbreak is not under control; WHO's chief points to slowing in most of the early hotspots while warning of the overall rise.[^15][^16]
